verdict.reasoning: Patient reports a headache that started yesterday and is located on the left side at the back of the head: “It started yesterday… It’s on the left side at the back.” Left occipital region is a reasonable clinical synonym.
Patient describes the headache as intense, throbbing, and building up gradually: “Just quite intense and kind of quite throbbing. It kind of built up gradually over a short period of time.”
When asked for a 0–10 score, patient answers: “Say about 8.”
Past headache history: Doctor: “And in the past, have you had any headaches before?” Patient: “Not really.” This supports no previous similar headaches.

Patient denies nausea, vomiting, and neurological symptoms: “Any nausea, vomiting, tingling, numbness, weakness anywhere?” Patient: “No, nothing.” She also denies blurred vision, eye pain, visual disturbance, and problems with light: “Any blurred vision or any pain over your eyes?” “No.” “Any funny lights… Any problems when you look into the light?” “No.” Phonophobia is not mentioned but is reasonably inferred as not reported.

Doctor asks about fever and rash: “Any high fever? Are you feeling shivery, sweaty?” Patient: “No, no fever.” “Any rashes at all?” Patient: “No.” No recent illness is not explicitly asked, but absence of any intercurrent illness is reasonably inferred from the review; no illness is mentioned.

Medication response: Doctor: “Have you taken any painkillers?” Patient: “I took some Nurofen yesterday.” Doctor: “And did that make any difference?” Patient: “Not really.” This supports non‑response to ibuprofen.
Sleep: Doctor: “And last night, did you manage to sleep through the night? Okay.” Patient: “Yes, I did.”

Positional/activity effects: “Has it been worse at any particular time of the day?” Patient: “No.” “Any difference if you lie down, stand up, bend over, cough or sneeze or anything like that?” Patient: “No.”
Eating and drinking: Doctor: “And if you've been eating and drinking, okay?” Patient: “Yes. Yes.”
Past medical history: Doctor: “And have you got any other medical problems?” Patient: “No, I haven't.”
Regular meds: Doctor: “Anything you take medication for?” Patient: “No, I don't.”
Patient explicitly states: “I took some Nurofen yesterday.” and clarifies “only the Nurofen I took yesterday, Ibuprofen.”
Doctor advises: “trying slightly stronger pain relief… You can take paracetamol along with that.” This supports paracetamol concurrently with the stronger analgesic.
Doctor asks: “Any over the counter medications or allergies?” Patient: “No, only the Nurofen I took yesterday, Ibuprofen.” This implies no known drug allergies.
Family history: “Anyone in your family got any medical problems?” Patient: “My mother's had hypertension…”
Same sentence: “…and she does get migraines.”
Living situation: Doctor: “Who do you live with at home?” Patient: “My partner.”
Occupation: Doctor: “And what's your job day to day?” Patient: “I'm a designer.”

The fact claims no missed work, but transcript says: Doctor: “Have you had to miss any work at all?” Patient: “No, but I don't feel that I'm finding it really hard to do any of my work or normal things.” Patient states difficulty performing work/normal tasks, so portraying only ‘not missed work’ omits this difficulty and is misleading but not directly contradictory. However, the specific claim about not missing work is accurate; therefore status should be SUPPORTED, not CONTRADICTION.
Smoking: Doctor: “And do you smoke at all normally?” Patient: “No, I don't.”
Alcohol: Doctor: “Do you drink any alcohol regularly?” Patient: “No.”
Drugs: Doctor: “And any other drugs?” Patient: “No.”
No examination findings are documented anywhere in the transcript; thus stating that no objective findings were documented is accurate.

Headache is acute, unilateral, and non‑responsive to NSAID with no red‑flag features reported. Transcript: onset yesterday, “just on the left side,” Nurofen “not really” helping, and explicit denials of fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, neuro deficits. Assessment wording is an appropriate clinical inference.
Migraine as a possible diagnosis is never explicitly mentioned by the doctor. Only the mother’s history of migraine is noted: “she does get migraines.” No diagnostic label is given in the assessment.
Tension-type headache is not mentioned or discussed as a possible diagnosis anywhere in the transcript.
Plan: “trying slightly stronger pain relief… and taking that regularly with food.” This matches trial of stronger analgesia with food.
Doctor advises: “Try and take rest, have lots of good hydration.”

Safety‑netting: “if the pain's getting worse or you get new symptoms, feel fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, or you keep getting episodes of the same type of thing, then we need to speak to you…” These are explicit red flag symptoms to monitor.

Follow‑up advice: “If it's getting worse or not settling in the next day or two, then certainly give us a call back when you try the medication that I prescribed…” This matches review if no improvement or worsening within 1–2 days.
